A frog wanders onto the judging table. The children declare it the winner for "Outstanding Participation." The frog appears entirely indifferent.
The prize ribbon blows away in a sudden gust of wind. The children spend the afternoon chasing it through the village.
{@Chief} accidentally awards the grand prize to the wrong child, then to the wrong parent, then to the schoolteacher. Eventually, the actual winner receives it.
Every child receives a trophy so large that nobody can carry theirs home. The adults reconsider their budgeting.
A child enters a drawing made by a coconut rolling through wet paint. The judges spend an embarrassing amount of time discussing its artistic significance.
The teacher explains that losing a contest does not mean being less worthy of kindness or respect. The children return to their games.
The winner congratulates the other children, and several promise to try again next year.
The adults agree to announce the judging criteria before future competitions. Nobody gets everything they want, but everyone understands the rules.
One child decides that (kid.he/she) would rather create things for fun than compete. The teacher supports the decision.
The parents go home, the ribbons are put away, and the children spend the evening laughing together.

intro.name: The contest
intro.text:
The village's children have been preparing for the annual {A} competition for weeks. Some have practiced every day. Others only joined because their friends were participating.
At last, the children gather to present their work. The parents and teachers are delighted - until someone asks who will receive the prize.
One parent insists that every child should be a winner. Another argues that choosing a single winner teaches children that effort and skill deserve recognition.
A third parent suggests canceling the entire ceremony. Nobody pays much attention to that suggestion.

text_only.reason: narrative: a parent's argument, not a skill gain

choices.label: GIVE EVERY CHILD THE SAME PRIZE
ASK THE CHILDREN WHAT THEY THINK

same.text: The teacher announces that every child will receive a ribbon. The children {cheer|look confused|whisper among themselves|immediately begin comparing ribbons}.

one.text: The judges carefully evaluate the entries and announce that one child will receive the grand prize.

multi.text: The judges decide to recognize different achievements, such as creativity, improvement, teamwork, and technical skill.

text_only.reason: an award category, not a skill gain

speak.text: The teacher gathers the children and asks what would make the competition feel fair to them. The answers are surprisingly varied.

sa1.text: The children are delighted. They proudly wear their ribbons and spend the rest of the day playing together.

sa2.text: One child asks why (kid.he/she) practiced for weeks if everyone was going to receive the same award. The teacher listens and promises clearer rules next time.

sa3.text: A shy child is relieved that nobody has to feel embarrassed. Another child admits that (kid.he/she) wanted to know how well (kid.he/she) actually did.

sa4.text: The children begin arguing over whose ribbon is shinier. The adults realize that equal prizes do not necessarily eliminate competition.

sa5.text: One child proudly announces that (kid.he/she) has won first place. So does every other child. {@Chief} has to explain that there cannot be thirty-seven first-place winners in a contest with only twelve entrants.

sa6.text: The children decide to exchange ribbons with one another. By evening, nobody remembers which ribbon belonged to whom.

on1.text: The winner is overjoyed, while the other children applaud. The teacher thanks everyone for their hard work.

on2.text: A disappointed child cries. The teacher comforts (kid.him/her) without pretending that losing is always pleasant.

on3.text: One parent accuses the judges of favoritism. The judges explain their criteria and offer to review the results.

on4.text: The winning child shares the prize with a friend. The judges remind everyone that the award still belongs to the winner.

on5.text: The winner admits that (kid.he/she) doesn't enjoy competing and only entered to make (kid.his/her) parents happy. The adults have a thoughtful conversation about expectations.

on6.text: A child who lost asks the winner for advice. The two begin practicing together for next year.

mu1.text: The children appreciate being recognized for different strengths. The ceremony ends peacefully.

mu2.text: One child receives the "Most Improved" award and asks, "Does that mean I was the worst before?" The teacher hurriedly explains what the award was meant to celebrate.

text_only.reason: narrative: what the award honours, not the Celebrating action

mu3.text: The judges invent so many categories that the ceremony lasts until sunset. Even the person handing out ribbons receives a ribbon.

mu4.text: Two children disagree about whether "Most Creative" is better than "Best Overall." The adults admit that the awards need clearer descriptions.

mu5.text: The children invent their own awards: "Best Friend," "Funniest Drawing," and "Most Likely to Eat the Prize." The teachers reluctantly allow the last one.

sp1.text: Most children vote for one winner, provided the rules are fair. The adults are surprised by their willingness to compete.

sp2.text: Most children prefer participation ribbons. The judges agree, but promise honest feedback for anyone who wants it.

sp3.text: The children propose a group challenge instead, where everyone works toward a shared goal.

sp4.text: The children disagree just as much as their parents. The teacher sighs. Apparently, democracy is complicated.

sp5.text: One child asks why adults are arguing about a contest that the children were enjoying perfectly well. The parents fall silent.

dispute.name: A parental dispute
dispute.text:
Two parents begin arguing so loudly that the children stop paying attention to the ceremony.
One parent {accuses the judges of favoritism|insists that (parent.his/her) child deserves a prize|demands a complete recount}. The other {defends the rules|argues for equal recognition|asks everyone to calm down}.
A child finally says, "Can we PLEASE just finish the contest?"
The parents {apologize|continue arguing until {@chief} intervenes|realize that they are embarrassing their children}.
